title: Validator
description: A check over one or more handoff kinds. `validator` spec §4 gives the four elements — purpose, inputs, implementation, result — and §9.2 the tag dictionary. The result type is boolean in v1; a score is reserved and built later, because a threshold set before run-to-run variance is measured is indistinguishable from noise (§4.2).

brief.description: The purpose, one line: which dimension this checks and what specifically. Required with no default — a registry of forty validators all named `check_trace_v2` is not searchable, and `validator` spec §9.3 check 2 makes absence a rejection rather than a warning because an unlabelled validator would default to being trusted.

dimension.description: `validator` spec §5.1. No default, for §9.3 check 2's reason.

strength.description: How far this check can be trusted, and it qualifies a PASS, never a failure (`validator` spec §5.4). `long_term_strong` is not a weaker `strong` — the rigour is the same and the timing is what differs. No default.

inputs.description: The handoff kinds this consumes, DECLARED rather than discovered, so a phase can dispatch only compatible validators and a reviewer can answer 'what does this actually read' without running it. The binding is many-to-many. The key is `inputs`: both this design and `handoff`'s called it `binds_to` in an early revision and no model has that key (docs/interfaces.md §4.3).

body.description: The implementation. A registered Python callable is NOT the interface — it cannot express a validator an agent is responsible for without a wrapper that runs an agent (`validator` spec §6.1). Present iff `members` is absent; that exclusivity is a named load-time check rather than an `if`/`then`, which produces a message nobody can act on.

agent.description:
The agent spec that carries this validator's environment — `validator` spec §8.2 row 1, *"bound to a real agent with a declared environment: that one"*. A NAME, resolved through `agent_specs`, because the environment already lives on the agent spec as `agent.env`; a second inline copy here would be two writers of one fact and they would diverge silently.

**Absent is legal** and takes §8.2's last row, the predefined global configuration — which is why this is not in `required`. Three of the four rows are reached by *not* naming one, so requiring it would make them unreachable.

**Present-but-unresolvable is fatal**, and the check is `closure`'s pass, not this schema's: the agent registry may not be loaded when this document is (main design §6.1 — *"resolve-during-load cannot see the far side of a binding"*). A name admitted here and resolved there is also registered with `agent_mgr`, since `task_graph/bootstrap.py` registers every `agent_specs` name — so a validator cannot name an agent the manager that runs it has never heard of.
agent.$comment: Read it through `spec_loader.validator_agent_of`, not as spec['agent']. Not `agent_of` — `closure.agent_of` reads a closure document and returns `str`, and neither raises on the wrong one. This comment named `validator.agent_of` for 55 seconds: it was true when written and withdrawn immediately after, which is why it now names an accessor in the same package as the schema.

args.description: This instance's parameters, reaching the body as `args.json` in its zone (`validator` design §10.6, D5). **Load-bearing**: criterion 12 is that two validators differing only in a parameter are two registry entries over one implementation, so one spec per instance is how a threshold is expressed at all. Deliberately unconstrained — the keys are the body's business, and a schema here would be this repository declaring another package's parameter vocabulary.

members.description: Where several checks combine: one combinator with a pluggable reducer, Inspect AI's `multi_scorer`. Top-level beside `reduce`, matching `ValidatorSpec` (`validator` design §3.2), which is the normative statement of the shape; spec §6.2's `composite(validators=[...], reduce=...)` is function-call prose, not a nesting. **Composition is flat** — a member that is itself a composite is rejected by a load-time check, as OpenAI's multigrader forbids outright. `minItems: 2` because a composite of one is a leaf with ceremony.

tags.description:
**Required, and so are two of its three fields.** Not a preference: `Tags` cannot be constructed empty, so an optional container would mean either a default `logic_source` — which is a default *trust* claim, and §9.3 check 2 forbids exactly that in the words 'an unlabelled validator would default to being trusted' — or `None`, which makes §5.3's cheap-first ordering crash rather than lose a value. Requiring the container while leaving its required fields optional would move the same gap one level deeper.

`validator` spec §9.2's dictionary, less `dimension` and `strength`, which are top-level here because `Validator` carries them as attributes rather than as tags (§4.1).

**Extra keys are allowed here and forbidden at the top level**, and the asymmetry is deliberate (`validator` design §3.5): a tag dictionary is where a site adds its own key, while a stray top-level field is a typo.

logic_source.description: Where the checking logic came from. The logic and the criterion are both external to the agent under test (`validator` spec §5.2).

cost.description: An order of magnitude. **A closed set, not free text**, because §5.3 orders a phase's validators by it cheap-first — an unordered value cannot be sorted, so a typo would silently become an unordered validator rather than a load error. Feeds the principle the whole system turns on: the expensive gate is very expensive, so anything catchable earlier must be caught earlier.

domain.description: Free-form, and a **list**: a validator legitimately spans more than one domain — a trace-analysis check is `trace` and `eval` — and §9.2's `trace`, `kernel`, `deploy`, `eval` is a menu of examples rather than a cardinality. A bare string is rejected on purpose: it is iterable, so it would pass a presence check and then iterate as characters, and `Tags.domain` is `tuple[str, ...]`, which pydantic refuses a string for. Admitting one here would let a document through this gate that the next gate rejects.
